work: Two Gods in Heaven: Jewish Concepts of God in Antiquity, 2020
edition: Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2020 (translated by Allison Brown); hardcover ISBN 9780691181325 (publisher page); ebook ISBN 9780691199894
chapter_or_section: Introduction: One God? (publisher sample, pp. 1-16)
quote_orig: The elevation of Jesus of Nazareth as the firstborn before all creation, the God incarnate, Son of God, Son of Man, the Messiah: all these basic Christological premises are not pagan or other kinds of aberrations; they are rooted in Second Temple Judaism, regardless of their specifically Christian character.
context_before: The New Testament took up these traditions that existed in Judaism, and did not reinvent but instead expanded and deepened them.
what_it_says: Schafer says the New Testament's high Christological titles for Jesus (firstborn, God incarnate, Son of God, Son of Man, Messiah) are rooted in Second Temple Judaism and are not pagan aberrations.
claim_supported: (D) background: Second Temple Judaism had room for a divine or semidivine second figure. Not a claim that Jesus himself claimed it.
scholar_qualification: He is describing the premises of NT Christology as Jewish in origin; he does not say Jesus claimed them about himself. He also says on pp. 8-9: “I expressly do not wish to get involved in the sophisticated New Testament discussion on the divinity of Jesus and its roots in early Judaism”. Schafer is a Jewish studies scholar who treats the Trinity as later development (after Nicaea and Constantinople).
limits: Read verbatim in the publisher's 23-page sample (front matter and Introduction). Line-break hyphens rejoined ('first-born' -> 'firstborn'); soft hyphens removed. Rest of book not read. Printed page confirmed from the running header 'One God? 5' and the sample's text order.

work: Two Gods in Heaven: Jewish Concepts of God in Antiquity, 2020

chapter_or_section: Introduction, p. 10: summary of Part I, ch. 7 'The Firstborn in the Prayer of Joseph'
quote_orig: The parallels to the godlike Jesus Christ, who as the firstborn before all creation was always with God, but who had to assume human form in order to complete the divine work of redemption, are obvious.
context_before: In the Prayer of Joseph, the highest angel Israel, as the firstborn before all creation, is identical with the human Jacob, patriarch of Israel. The highest angel in heaven is hence in reality a human being, who as the sole creature was with God in heaven prior to all creation.
what_it_says: Schafer says the Jewish Prayer of Joseph figure parallels the Christian Jesus as firstborn before creation, sent to complete redemption.
claim_supported: (D) background; also (E) a parallel drawn by Schafer, not a claim about Jesus' self-understanding.
scholar_qualification: 'Parallels' is his word: he identifies similarity between a Jewish text and Christian Christology, and does not say the Gospels depend on it or that Jesus identified himself with it. The passage is about the Prayer of Joseph's figure, not about what Jesus said.
limits: As J7-01. The quote is about 37 words, within the 25-90 range.

quote_orig: I do not see any evidence in the sources of Palestinian Judaism for the Son of God as a second deity next to the biblical God of creation, and I presume that the usurpation of the Jewish Son of Man by the New Testament-Jesus as the Son of Man who will come with the clouds of heaven and is enthroned at the right hand of God

work: The Sovereignty of the Son of Man: Reading Mark 2, 2010
edition: In Annette Weissenrieder and Robert B. Coote (eds.), The Interface of Orality and Writing (WUNT 260), Tubingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2010, pp. 353-62; volume ISBN 978-3-16-150445-7 (Mohr Siebeck page)
chapter_or_section: Opening paragraph of the essay (as reproduced in a blog)
page: 354 (page marker placed by the blogger after the sentence; essay pp. 353-62)
quote_orig: My simple answer is that the “Son of Man” was on Jesus’ lips, because he was a first-century, Palestinian Jew, and “Son of Man” was the name that these Jews used for their expected divine-human (Christological!) redeemer.
context_before: This article, in its present form, is intended as an answer to the question of “how the ‘Son of Man’ . . . came to appear on Jesus’ lips in Mark’s Gospel, or for that matter in the tradition as a whole.”
what_it_says: Boyarin's answer: Jesus used 'Son of Man' because it was the name first-century Palestinian Jews gave to their expected divine-human redeemer.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus himself speaks of himself with a divine-human title (as Boyarin reads it), plus (D) background.
scholar_qualification: This is the strongest Boyarin statement on Jesus' own use of the title that I found. It is his reconstruction of the title's meaning in Jesus' time, not a text in which Jesus says 'I am God'. He treats the 'divine-human' sense as a Jewish category, and speaks of Mark's Jesus separately (J7-17, J7-18). Note that he also calls the redeemer's authority 'delegated by God' (J7-16).
limits: The essay itself is on Boyarin's academia.edu page, which returned 403 to me, so I did not read the printed text. The text here is a blogger's reproduction with page markers. Cover is for Jewish Gospels; no cover for this volume was downloaded.

chapter_or_section: Reading of Mark 2:5-10 (forgiveness of sins)
page: page unknown (essay pp. 353-62; the blogger's markers put it between '(354)' and '(359 f)')
quote_orig: Once we have excluded the possibility of “the Son of Man” being simply, another way of saying “I,” then I think it must be conceded that it is a title, here. The Son of Man has authority (obviously delegated by God) to do God’s work of the forgiving of sins on earth.
context_before: Mark 2:10 ('the Son of man has authority on earth to forgive sins') is the crux, and Boyarin rejects the reading 'Son of Man' = 'I' for it. (My summary.)
what_it_says: Boyarin reads 'Son of Man' in Mark 2:10 as a title, and says the Son of Man's authority to forgive sins is delegated by God.

scholar_qualification: He says the authority is 'obviously delegated by God', which is a limit: the figure acts with God's authority, not as God himself. He does not say the Mark 2 scene is Jesus claiming YHWH's identity. The Ezekiel 'son of man' point is not addressed in what I read.

chapter_or_section: Discussion of Ephesians 1:21 and the NT 'two powers' themes
quote_orig: Many “two powers” themes have come together. Jesus is raised from the dead and enthroned as Christ far above the status of any man or angel. He is sovereign in this age and the age to come, a claim explicitly reserved for God according to rabbinic tradition. Furthermore, Christ has been exalted beyond any title that can be named, implying that he has been awarded the secret name of God.
